terms.definition: A training-time attack on knowledge distillation, where someone corrupts the transfer of behavior from a larger model to a smaller one.
An AI system that can learn, reason, and apply knowledge across many tasks at a human level or beyond, rather than one narrow job.
Systems that pursue goals by planning steps, using tools, and adjusting their actions from feedback, with little ongoing human direction.
The work of making an AI system's objectives and behavior match human intentions, rules, and values.
Shared tests used to compare models on tasks such as question answering, vision, coding, or instruction following.
The skill of working with AI productively: knowing what it can and cannot do, checking its output, and using it responsibly.
Research and practice aimed at making AI systems reliable and preventing them from causing harm, including in unexpected situations.
The combined software, hardware, and compute used across the AI lifecycle, from data and training to deployment.
The full path of an AI application: prepare data, train a model, test it, deploy it, and keep it running.
A finite sequence of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task.
Many organizations relying on the same or very similar models, algorithms, or training data.
A group of AI systems that share information and coordinate what they do.
The field, named in 1955 by John McCarthy, concerned with building machines that can perform tasks that require intelligence.
A neural-network method that lets a model weigh the parts of its input that matter most for the current output.
The training procedure that sends a model's error backward through the network to update the connections that caused it.
Graphs that show how variables influence one another, with probabilities on those relationships.
Systematic skew in a system's results that advantages or disadvantages particular groups of people.
Datasets so large or complex that ordinary data tools struggle to process them.
Software that holds a conversation with a person, usually by text or voice.
Software whose code is kept private so the public cannot inspect, change, or reuse it. Also called proprietary software.
AI that interprets images and video, such as recognizing objects or scenes.
How much input a model can consider at once while doing a task.
Training by comparing similar and dissimilar examples so the model learns what belongs together.
Expanding a training set by making altered copies of existing examples instead of collecting new ones.
Searching large datasets for patterns and trends with statistics and machine learning.
An attack that inserts, changes, or mislabels training examples so the resulting model is corrupted or secretly steered.
A model that predicts by asking a series of yes-or-no questions about features until it reaches an answer.
Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn complex patterns from data.
Generative models that create content, often images, by learning to remove noise that was added to data.
Simplifying data by using fewer variables while keeping the most important information.
Lists of numbers that represent items such as words or images so that similar items sit near each other.
Combining several models so the group's prediction is stronger than any single model's.
Building and deploying AI so that it respects fairness, transparency, human values, and social well-being.
A program that applies a stored body of facts and if-then rules to reach conclusions in a narrow domain.
Methods that make a model's decisions understandable to people instead of leaving them opaque.
Training a shared model across many devices or servers while each party's data stays where it is.
Learning a new task from only a small number of examples.
Extra training of an already trained model on data for a particular task or domain.
A large model, often a transformer, trained on broad data so it can be adapted to many later tasks.
A general-purpose model at or near the current leading edge of capability.
AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio, code, or video.
A pair of networks, a generator and a discriminator, trained against each other so the generator produces realistic synthetic data.
A family of large language models that use the transformer architecture to continue or write text from a prompt.
A chip built to do many calculations at once, first for graphics and now widely used to train and run AI models.
Output that is false or made up but presented as if it were true.
An approach that puts human needs, values, and well-being at the center of how AI is built and used.
The study and design of how people operate and interact with computer systems.
Systems that keep a person in the process to review, correct, or approve what the AI does.
A setting chosen before training starts, rather than learned from the data during training.
A very large technology company that runs huge data-center networks and can expand cloud computing and storage quickly.
Using a trained model to make a prediction or decision on new data.
How well a person can follow the reasons behind a model's output.
A simple method that classifies or predicts a point from the labels of the nearest examples in the training set.
A database that stores facts as entities linked by relationships.
A model trained on very large amounts of text so it can understand and produce language.
A lower-dimensional representation in which the important patterns of complex data are encoded.
The practices for deploying, monitoring, and maintaining applications built on large language models.
A score of how far a model's predictions are from the correct answers, used to guide training.
AI methods that learn patterns from data instead of relying only on hand-written rules.
A model of a sequence in which the next step depends only on the current state, not on the earlier path.
Practices that combine machine learning, software engineering, and operations so models can be deployed and maintained reliably.
A mathematical or computational stand-in for a real process, used to find patterns or make predictions.
A drop in a model's accuracy over time because live data no longer matches the data it was trained on.
Systems that can take in and produce more than one kind of data, such as text, images, audio, and video.
AI focused on understanding, interpreting, and generating human language.
A model made of connected layers of simple units, loosely inspired by neurons, that transform input into output.
The method that updates a model's settings during training so its errors get smaller.
When a model fits the training examples too closely, including noise, and then does poorly on new data.
A model released with enough of its weights, code, data documentation, and tools that others can run, inspect, and modify it.
A model whose learned weights are published so others can download and run it, even if other training materials stay private.
Software whose source code is available for people to view, use, and change.
A value inside a model that is adjusted during training and then used at inference time.
Using data and models to estimate what is likely to happen next.
Writing and structuring the instructions given to a language model so the output is more useful.
An attack that hides instructions in input so a language model ignores its intended rules or task.
A method that retrieves outside information and gives it to a language model before the model writes an answer.
A model built to work through harder problems in explicit intermediate steps rather than jumping straight to an answer.
Learning by trying actions and getting rewards or penalties, then favoring actions that work better.
Principles and practices for developing and deploying AI in ways that are safe, fair, and accountable.
The field that designs machines to carry out physical tasks, often using engineering, computer science, and AI.
The ability to reason about 3D space: where things are, how they move, and how they interact.
Training in which the model creates its own learning signal from raw data, without human labels for every example.
Interpreting meaning in language from how words and phrases relate to each other.
Observed relationships that describe how model performance changes as size, data, and compute grow.
Training on examples that already include the correct output.
Data created by a program or simulation rather than collected from real events.
A multi-dimensional array of numbers used to store data and model values.
Splitting text into smaller pieces, called tokens, that a language model can process.
Earlier AI that depended on explicit rules and human-encoded knowledge rather than learning from data.
The examples used to teach a machine-learning model a task.
Starting from a model trained on one task and adapting it to a related task.
A neural architecture that uses attention to relate all parts of an input to each other, rather than reading them only in order.
Alan Turing's 1950 proposal for judging a machine by whether a person can tell its conversation apart from a human's.
Training on data that has no supplied labels, so the model has to find structure by itself.
A database built to store embeddings and search for the nearest ones quickly.
A transformer adapted to treat an image as a sequence of patches and analyze it.
The learned numbers in a neural network that control how strongly units influence one another.
Performing a task or recognizing a category without having been trained on labeled examples of that specific task.
